options.text: Reading every word slowly and carefully
options.why: This is close reading, not skimming.

options.text: Hunting for one particular word or number
options.why: This is scanning.
Skimming is a silent, fast way of reading.

options.text: Reading quickly to get the general idea

hints: Think of skimming a stone: it touches only the surface.
Skimming is about the big picture.
Which choice talks about the general idea?
items.explanation: To skim is to run your eyes over a text quickly to get the main idea.

items.prompt: You need the date of the school fair in a long newsletter. What is the best method?

options.text: Scan for the word fair and for numbers
Read every word from the start
options.why: This would take too long when you want only one detail.
The date may not be in the first line.

options.text: Ask a friend what it says
options.why: You can find it yourself faster by scanning.

hints: You only want one fact.
Your eyes should hunt for a key word.
Look for the word fair and for a date.
items.explanation: When you want a single detail, scan for key words or numbers instead of reading everything.

items.prompt: Sort each task by the reading method it needs.

items.text: Decide if a book looks interesting
Get the gist of an article
Find a word in a glossary

hints: Skim is for the big idea. Scan is for one detail.
A train time is a single detail.
Start with Get the gist of an article. Do you want a detail or the whole idea?
items.explanation: Skimming gives you an overview. Scanning finds a particular detail such as a time, name or number.

items.prompt: You want to find every page that mentions lava in a book. Where should you look first?

options.why: A glossary explains hard words but does not list every page.
The title page gives the book's title and author, not the pages for a topic.
Lava might be mentioned in any chapter.

hints: An index lists topics and page numbers.
It is arranged in alphabetical order.
Look at the back of the book under L.
items.explanation: The index lists topics in alphabetical order with the pages where they appear.

items.prompt: Match each book feature to what it helps you do.
pairs: find every page about a topic
check the meaning of a hard word
see what a section is about
hints: Each feature has its own job.
The glossary is like a mini dictionary.
Start with contents: it shows chapters in order.
items.explanation: Book features help readers find and understand information quickly.

items.prompt: Choose all the parts of a page that help you skim a non-fiction text quickly.

options.text: The last word of every line
options.why: Reading only line endings gives no meaning.
A page number does not tell you about the content.

hints: Skimming needs quick clues to what a section is about.
Look at things that stand out on the page.
Cross out items that give no meaning.
items.explanation: Headings, bold words and captions stand out and show what each part is about.

items.prompt: Dewi must reach the museum by 10:30. Using the timetable, which is the latest bus she can take?

options.why: Bus 14 would arrive early, but a later bus also gets her there in time.
Bus 31 arrives at 10:40, which is after 10:30.
Bus 45 arrives at 10:50, which is too late.

hints: Scan the Arrives column.
Cross out any bus that arrives after 10:30.
Of the buses left, which leaves latest?
items.explanation: Buses 14 and 22 arrive before 10:30. Bus 22 leaves later, so it is the latest she can take.

Leaves

figure.alt: Timetable. Bus 14 leaves 08:50 and arrives 09:35. Bus 22 leaves 09:20 and arrives 10:05. Bus 31 leaves 09:50 and arrives 10:40. Bus 45 leaves 10:05 and arrives 10:50.

items.prompt:
Scan the note for the correct room number.

Hi Tom, the art club has moved! We meet on Thursday at 3:45 in Room 12, not Room 8. Bring an apron.
hints: Scan for the word Room.
There are two room numbers. Read what each one is for.
One is where the club moved to. The other is the old place.
items.explanation: The club moved to Room 12. The note says it is not Room 8.

items.prompt: Which question is best answered by scanning rather than skimming?

options.text: What is the whole article about?
options.why: This needs skimming for the main idea.

options.text: In what year did the bridge open?
Does the writer like the bridge?
options.why: This needs careful reading of the writer's tone.
This needs a quick look at headings, which is skimming.

hints: Scanning is for a single detail.
A year is a number you can hunt for.
Look for the question with one clear answer.
items.explanation: A date is one small detail. You can scan for four digits near the word bridge.

items.prompt: Put the steps for finding an answer in a long text in order.
items: Read the question and pick the key words
Skim the headings to find the right section
Scan that section for the key words
Read the sentences around the key words closely
Check your answer matches the question
hints: Start by deciding what you are looking for.
Narrow down from the whole text to a section, then to a word.
Close reading comes after you have found the place.
items.explanation: Choose key words first, skim to the right section, scan for the words, then read carefully and check.

items.prompt: To get the general idea of a text quickly, you ___ it. To find one fact, you ___ it.
hints: Skim is about the big idea.
Scan is about a single fact.
Fill the first gap with the big-idea word.
items.explanation: You skim to get the gist and scan to pick out a single fact.

items.prompt: Maya is writing about tides. She has three library books. Which method is most efficient?

options.text: Read each book from cover to cover
options.why: This takes a very long time.
She might miss useful facts from the others.

options.text: Look up tides in each index, then read only those pages
Look at the covers and choose the prettiest
options.why: Looks do not tell you about the facts.

hints: She needs facts from more than one source.
Which book feature points to a topic?
Use the index first.
items.explanation: Using each index finds the relevant pages quickly, so she reads only what she needs.
